topic: Mastering Discrete Convolutions: The Art of Sliding and Summing
target_audience: Undergraduate STEM students (Computer Science, Engineering, or Mathematics)

sections.title: The Big Picture: Why Convolve?
lecture_lines: Convolution combines two signals into a single new output.
It powers image filters, audio effects, and computer vision.
A sharp image blurs by averaging pixels with neighbors.
animations: Display two abstract signals (blue pulse and yellow bell curve) side-by-side.
Pulse a sharp image icon and an audio wave icon with #00FFFF highlights.
An eye icon looks at a pixel grid; highlight specific cells with #FF00FF.
Display a sharp 8x8 pixel grid; apply a blur effect visually.
Highlight a 3x3 region; show numbers flowing from neighbors to the center pixel.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Signals as Sequences
lecture_lines: Discrete signals are simple sequences of numerical values.
We have an input signal and a filter kernel.
Signals are mapped to integer indices on a graph.
animations: Show a horizontal axis with vertical bars representing [1, 2, 3, 2, 1] in #FFFFFF.
Label the sequence "x[n]" in green #00FF00 above the bars.
Show a smaller sequence [0.5, 1, 0.5] labeled "h[n]" in yellow #FFFF00 below.

sections.title: The Mechanics: Flip, Shift, and Multiply
lecture_lines: Convolution follows a simple three-step physical process.
First, we flip the filter kernel horizontally.
Next, we shift the flipped filter across the input.
We multiply overlapping values and sum the results.
This sum becomes the output at that specific position.
animations: Mirror the yellow h[n] bars across the y-axis to show h[-k].
Slide the h[-k] bars horizontally from left to right along the x-axis.
Highlight overlap with #00FF00; show "x" symbols between overlapping bars.
Display a Sigma symbol \u03a3 and show the products summing into a single value.
Plot the result as a new dot on a second axis below.

sections.title: 1D Graphical Walkthrough
lecture_lines: Let’s visualize two pulses colliding and passing through.
As they start overlapping, the output value begins growing.
The peak occurs when the signals achieve maximum overlap.
The output fades as the signals move apart.
The result represents the mathematical area of their overlap.
animations: Static blue rectangular pulse x[k] on a white horizontal axis.
Yellow rectangular pulse h[-k] starts at the far left, moving right.
Slide yellow pulse into blue; begin drawing a red line for the output.
Fully overlap pulses; red output line reaches its peak height.
Slide yellow pulse completely past blue; red output line returns to zero.

sections.title: 2D Application: Digital Image Filters
lecture_lines: Images are two-dimensional grids of intensity values.
A small matrix, called a kernel, slides over pixels.
Different kernel values produce blur, sharpen, or edge effects.
Edge detectors highlight rapid changes in pixel brightness.
These 2D convolutions are the core of modern AI.
animations: Show a 5x5 grid of gray numbers (0-255) representing image pixels.
A 3x3 yellow frame slides step-by-step across the 5x5 grid.
As the frame moves, the center pixel in a separate output grid changes color.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Impact
lecture_lines: Remember the workflow: Flip the filter, shift, and sum.
Convolution is the language of linear systems and signals.
It transforms raw data into meaningful, processed information.
animations: Flash icons for Flip (Mirror), Shift (Arrow), and Sum (Sigma) in #00FFFF.
Show a simplified CNN layer diagram with connections pulsing.
Display a smartphone icon surrounded by rapid mathematical equations.
